title: How to create product color variants without photographing every color
summary: Learn how to create accurate product color variants from one source image without photographing and editing every colorway separately.
body_markdown:
One T-shirt in one color is one photography job. The same T-shirt, from multiple angles, in eight different colors, can quickly become dozens.


For a small e‑commerce business, a seemingly simple product variation can create a lot of work. Every new color can mean another product to prepare, photograph, edit, resize, check, organize, and attach to the correct listing variant.


And visually, you're trying to recreate almost exactly the same image each time.


Same product.


Same angle.


Same position.


Same background.


Same lighting.


But a different color.


If the product itself hasn't changed, ****[the production workflow](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-create-repeatable-product-image-workflow) **shouldn't have to start again from zero** . For products where color is the main difference between variants,[AI recoloring](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/change-color-image) can let you start with one reliable product image and create the real colorways you sell from that source.


The principle is simple: **Photograph the structure once. Produce the colorways from it.**


[Photoroom’s Recolor tool](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) is designed for this exact scenario. Upload a product, select a color, and Photoroom will recolor your product image while preserving the details that matter, like texture and shadows—without a separate photography workflow.


## Table of Contents


## The fastest way to generate multiple color variants of a product image for your product catalog


Imagine you sell a sweatshirt in six different colors. If you photograph every color separately, you're not just taking six photographs.


You’re repeating:


**setup → positioning → photography → background removal → crop → sizing → shadow → export → upload**


six times.


If every color also needs three listing images, you're now managing 18 assets. Multiply that across a[growing product catalog](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-scale-product-image-creation-e-commerce) , and[product color image variants](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/product-variant-image-generation) become a production problem.


For a large e‑commerce team, repeated photography might simply be part of the production budget. For a small seller, the same work competes with everything else required to get the product live.


But if color is the only thing that’s changed between your SKUs, you might not need to reproduce the entire image-production process. Instead, you can follow a simple workflow:


**Photograph the product once → define the real colorways → generate variants → validate color + product details → attach to correct variants → publish**


Here’s how.


### 1. Start with one reliable source image


The quality of the e‑commerce color variants you create depends on the image you start with. Choose a source image that clearly represents the product's:


-


Shape


-


Proportions


-


Materials


-


Texture


-


Construction


-


Stitching


-


Folds


-


Logos


-


Trims


-


Important details


[Good lighting](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/image-brightener) also matters because highlights and shadows convey the product's shape and material.


You're not trying to create a generic silhouette and fill it with different colors. You're trying to preserve the physical characteristics of the real product while changing the part that actually varies between SKUs.


Think of the source image as the structural truth of the product. The color is the variable.


### 2. Define the colors you actually sell


Before generating anything, list the real product variants. Suppose the source sweatshirt is navy and your actual catalog includes:


-


Navy


-


Black


-


Burgundy


-


Forest Green


-


Cream


Those are the images you need. You don't need to create twenty clothing color variants simply because the tool can create them.


There's an important distinction here:


-


**Color correction** means adjusting an image so the color more accurately represents the physical product.


-


**Color variant creation** means creating an image representing another real, purchasable colorway of the same product.


-


**Creative recoloring** means experimenting with different colors, whether or not those products exist.


All three can be useful. But for e‑commerce listing imagery, they're not interchangeable. Only show a color as a product variant if that's a product the customer can actually buy. The goal isn't creative recoloring. It's complete catalog coverage with less production work.


Photoroom has tools for each of the first two jobs.[The color changer](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/change-color-image) gives you manual control over hue, saturation, brightness, and contrast. That makes it the right tool for color correction.[Recolor](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) is built for[creating different color variants](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/product-variant-image-generation) of a single product. It uses AI to replace the product’s color entirely while preserving its texture, folds, and lighting.


In practice: if your navy sweatshirt photo looks slightly purple on screen, use the color changer. If you need an image of the forest green version, use Recolor.


### 3. Change the product color in your photo to create each colorway


Once you have a strong source image and know which variants you need, you can generate them using the original source image.


[Photoroom's Recolor tool](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) uses AI to identify the product and change its color while retaining visual characteristics such as texture, folds, lighting, and shadows.


So instead of:


-


**Photograph black → edit black**


-


**Photograph green → edit green**


-


**Photograph burgundy → edit burgundy**


you can move toward:


**photograph black product → generate green + burgundy**


The background, composition, product position, and other presentation choices can remain consistent. That makes each image more useful when its purpose is to let shoppers compare variants.


### 4. Keep everything except the color consistent


There's another advantage to creating variants from a shared source: consistency becomes much easier. This is a case where reducing production variation can improve the shopping experience and save time.


Imagine a product gallery where the black T-shirt is photographed slightly closer than the red one, the blue version sits higher in the frame, and the green one has slightly different lighting.


None of those differences tell the shopper anything useful. They're production inconsistencies.


For color variants, the ideal comparison often retains these factors across images:


-


Product


-


Composition


-


Scale


-


[Lighting](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/image-brightener)


-


[Background](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/instant-backgrounds)


And simply changes the color.


That makes the one thing that’s different between your products much easier to see.


### 5. Validate color and product details against the real SKU


Generating a convincing color isn't enough. The image can look professionally produced and still be inaccurate. This matters because shoppers make decisions based on what they see on screen—the product they receive needs to match what they saw on your storefront.


Start with the most precise color reference you have. If your product specification includes a hex code, Pantone reference, or supplier color card, use it.[Photoroom’s Recolor tool](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) lets you choose a color with a color picker or enter a specific color value, so you can generate each variant from the exact color on file instead of matching it by eye.


After generating a variant, compare it with the physical product, its color specification, or another reliable product reference. Check these details of your product photo for accuracy:


-


Hue


-


Brightness


-


Saturation


-


Material appearance


-


Shadows and highlights


A dark green shouldn't become teal. Cream shouldn't become white. Burgundy shouldn't become bright red. **The goal isn't to generate a plausible color. It's to accurately represent the real colorway.**


Then, check that other product details remain stable. This becomes particularly important for products where changing the color affects how texture or material appears. If your red handbag is made of the same leather as the black version, the generated image should still accurately convey that material.


Along with texture and material,[check for accuracy](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-fix-inaccurate-ai-product-images) in details like:


-


Shape


-


Stitching


-


Trims


-


Proportions


-


Seams


-


Folds


-


Hardware


-


Patterns


-


Logos


-


Labels


-


Construction details


If another colorway actually uses different hardware or trim, simply recoloring the source image may not be sufficient. At that point, color isn't the only variable anymore. You need a source that accurately represents those additional differences too.


### 6. Bulk recolor product images as your catalog grows


The more products and colors you sell, the faster the workload multiplies.


Consider:


**20 products × 6 colors × 3 images = 360 finished assets**


[Photoroom's research with 1,356 e‑commerce sellers](https://www.photoroom.com/industry-trends/product-photography-cost-for-smbs) found that sellers historically spent a median of 15 minutes editing each product image. At that pace, those 360 assets amount to 90 hours spent recreating images that differ only in color.


If multiple products or images need the same type of recoloring, you can apply Recolor to up to 250 images at once in[Photoroom’s Batch mode](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) .


That lets you move away from:


**open → recolor → export → repeat**


toward:


**select source assets → generate required variants → review → publish**


The objective isn't simply to make individual edits faster. It's to[reduce the amount of repeated production](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-scale-product-image-creation-e-commerce) that occurs every time the catalog adds another colorway. **Color options shouldn't slow down how quickly products reach the store.**


### 7. Connect each image to the correct variant


Producing the images is only part of the workflow. They also need to be associated with the correct products.


If your listing offers:


-


Black


-


Green


-


Cream


-


Burgundy


Selecting Green should show the shopper imagery representing the green product. Accuracy matters here too. A perfect green image attached to the burgundy variant is still a bad product experience.


For Shopify users,[Photoroom's Shopify integration](https://www.photoroom.com/integrations/shopify) lets you work directly with your store’s product images and variants. Choose the product image, select the colors you sell, and[Photoroom generates each color version](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) while keeping the same lighting, framing, and product details. You can then associate each image with its matching product option.


That can reduce another repetitive step: generating files separately and then manually figuring out which asset belongs to which SKU.


Before publishing, check:


**generated color → real SKU → Shopify variant**


## Which products are good candidates for AI recoloring?


This workflow is most straightforward when the product remains physically the same, and color is the primary difference between variants.


Examples of good candidates for AI recoloring include:


-


Basic apparel


-


Accessories


-


Simple footwear


-


Home textiles


-


Some furniture


-


Simple packaged or manufactured goods


[Photoroom's Recolor](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) is currently designed primarily for single-color products, though products with neutral trims like black, white, or gray can also work well.


More complex products—such as those with multiple colors, patterns, and structural changes—may require a different approach. A “blue” shoe with different laces, sole, stitching, and logo treatment isn't simply a recolored version of the black SKU.


Let the product decide the workflow, not the other way around.


## When should you create multiple product images for each colorway?


An e‑commerce listing may need more than one image for each color.


You might have a:


-


Primary product image


-


Side view


-


Back view


-


Detail image


-


[Lifestyle image](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-create-lifestyle-product-photos-with-ai)


If you have reliable source photography for those views, the same principle can be applied across them.


Instead of photographing every angle in every color, photograph one source image for each angle, then[produce the associated color variants](https://www.photoroom.com/use-cases/product-variant-image-generation) :


-


**Front source → color variants**


-


**Side source → color variants**


-


**Back source → color variants**


This can dramatically reduce the number of photographs required while still giving shoppers useful coverage of each color option.


But don't generate a view where a source image doesn’t exist. Recoloring a visible side of a product is different from asking AI to invent what the unseen back looks like. If the back of the real product has a pocket, a seam, or a label the AI couldn't see, shoppers end up making decisions based on details that don't exist. When the product arrives and doesn't match, you pay for it in returns, support requests, and lost trust, which can easily outweigh the time you saved producing the image.


Reuse what you know. Don't manufacture product information you don't have.


## How to launch new colorways without another photoshoot


This workflow becomes especially useful for businesses that add colors more frequently than they add entirely new products.


Imagine you sell a core sweatshirt year-round. Spring introduces three new colors. Autumn introduces another four. Traditionally,[every seasonal color launch](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-scale-product-images-peak-season) can trigger another round of photography.


[Photoroom's research](https://www.photoroom.com/industry-trends/product-photography-cost-for-smbs) found that traditional product photography costs $25 to $500 per image, plus $150 to $300 per studio hour. For the sweatshirt above, seven seasonal colors with three listing images each means 21 new images a year. That's $525 to $10,500 in photography.


But if the physical product hasn't changed, you may be able to use the existing product photography as your source and create imagery for the new real colorways. That means your original photography investment continues to deliver value as the catalog evolves.


For a small e‑commerce business, this can change the economics of offering more variants.


Instead of:


**new color = new production**


you move closer to:


**new color = new validated output from an existing production system**


That’s how[women’s workwear brand Ameliora](https://www.photoroom.com/customer-stories/ameliora) manages its catalog. It offers five core shirt silhouettes in up to 15 colors each, including 8 colors of its top-selling Dawn shirt and 14 of its Boyfriend shirt. For a small team, reshooting every new color was prohibitively expensive. Editing colors manually in Photoshop was slow and error-prone, too: buttons changed color by accident, and textures flattened, making fabrics look artificial.


Now founder Adrienne Kronovet uses[Recolor](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) to create each colorway from a single product image, applying each shirt’s exact hex color code while preserving the fabric’s folds, stitching, and shading. “I can simply say, ‘change it to black,’ ‘change it to white,’ or ‘change it to grey,’” she says. Accurate color has also given shoppers the confidence to buy beyond neutrals: Ameliora reports a 30% increase in sales variety.


## When should you still photograph every color?


AI recoloring isn't the right solution for every product. Photograph the real variant when color is accompanied by meaningful physical differences, or when accurate representation can't be reliably achieved from another colorway.


That might include:


-


Complex patterns


-


Different materials


-


Unique textures


-


Variant-specific hardware


-


Embroidery or printed graphics


-


Transparency or reflective finishes


-


Subtle colors that are difficult to reproduce accurately


-


Products where color interacts strongly with the material


You may also choose real photography for hero campaign imagery where exact art direction or physical interaction with the product matters.


The goal isn't to eliminate photography. It's to stop repeating the entire photography production process when the only meaningful product difference doesn't require it.


## Create eight product color variants without eight photography workflows


Small e‑commerce businesses need the same thing larger retailers do: accurate imagery for every product customers can buy.


They just don't necessarily have[the photography budget](https://www.photoroom.com/blog/how-to-take-professional-product-photos-without-studio) , studio time, or production team to recreate the same image every time a product launches in another color.


When color is the only meaningful difference, you can change the production model:


1.


Start with a reliable source image.


2.


Preserve the product's structure, texture, lighting, and presentation.


3.


Generate only the colorways that actually exist.


4.


Then validate each one against the product you're selling.


**You shouldn't need another photoshoot simply because the product comes in another color.**


With[Photoroom Recolor](https://www.photoroom.com/tools/recolor) , small e‑commerce businesses can create real product color variants from existing images,[generate variants in Batch](https://www.photoroom.com/batch) , and work with color options inside[connected Shopify workflows](https://www.photoroom.com/integrations/shopify) without rebuilding the entire photography process for every SKU.
